This file implements the LedgerMaster class, which is a core component of the XRPL server responsible for managing the lifecycle, state, and history of ledgers. Overall, this file is central to the operation of distributed consensus in the XRPL node software, coordinating ledger agreement, transaction application, and network communication during consensus rounds.

The most recent ledger that the server believes the network reached consensus on. Different servers can arrive at a different conclusion about the last closed ledger. This is a consequence of Byzantanine failure. The purpose of validations is to resolve the differences between servers and come to a common conclusion about which last closed ledger is authoritative.

## Consensus ##

A distributed agreement protocol. Ripple uses the consensus process to solve the problem of double-spending.

## Validation ##

A signed statement indicating that it built a particular ledger as a result of the consensus process.

## Proposal ##

A signed statement of which transactions it believes should be included in the next consensus ledger.

## Ledger Header ##

The "ledger header" is the chunk of data that hashes to the ledger's hash. It contains the sequence number, parent hash, hash of the previous ledger, hash of the root node of the state tree, and so on.

content: For consensus to be considered healthy, the peers on the network should largely remain in sync with one another. It is particularly important for the validators to remain in sync, because that is required for participation in consensus. However, the network tolerates some validators being out of sync.  Fundamentally, network health is a function of validators reaching consensus on sets of recently submitted transactions.

This file implements the NegativeUNLVote class, which manages the voting process for the Negative Unique Node List (Negative UNL) in the XRPL consensus protocol. The Negative UNL is a mechanism to temporarily exclude unreliable validators from consensus without removing them permanently. The class provides methods to: 1) Collect and score validator performance over a configurable interval using validation history; 2) Identify candidates for disabling (adding to Negative UNL) or re-enabling (removing from Negative UNL) based on their reliability scores and protocol thresholds; 3) Randomly select candidates for action in a deterministic way; 4) Construct and add transactions to the ledger to modify the Negative UNL; 5) Track and manage new validators to avoid disabling them prematurely; 6) Log relevant actions and errors for debugging. The logic ensures that only validators with sufficient local validation activity participate in voting, and that the Negative UNL does not exceed protocol-defined limits. The class interacts with the ledger, validation records, and the transaction set to coordinate Negative UNL changes as part of the consensus process.

Byzantine failures are resolved as follows. If there is a supermajority ledger, then a minority of validators will discover that the consensus round is proceeding on a different ledger than they thought. These validators will become desynced, and switch to a strategy of trying to acquire the consensus ledger.

If there is no majority ledger, then starting on the next consensus round there will not be a consensus on the last closed ledger. Another avalanche process is started.

The consensus ledger and

The last validated ledger.

The fee voting mechanism takes place every 256 ledgers ("voting ledgers"). In a voting ledger, each validator takes a position on what they think the fees should be. The consensus process converges on the majority position, and in subsequent ledgers a new fee schedule is enacted.

## Consensus

The Ripple consensus algorithm allows distributed participants to arrive at the same answer for yes/no questions. The canonical case for consensus is whether or not a particular transaction is included in the ledger. Fees present a more difficult challenge, since the decision on the new fee is not a yes or no question.

To convert validators' positions on fees into a yes or no question that can be converged in the consensus process, the following algorithm is used:

In the ledger before a voting ledger, validators send proposals which also

include the values they think the network should use for the new fee schedule.

# RCL Consensus

This directory holds the types and classes needed to connect the generic consensus algorithm to the rippled-specific instance of consensus.

`RCLCxTx` adapts a `SHAMapItem` transaction.

`RCLCxTxSet` adapts a `SHAMap` to represent a set of transactions.

`RCLCxLedger` adapts a `Ledger`.

`RCLConsensus` is implements the requirements of the generic

`Consensus` class by connecting to the rest of the `rippled`

application.

ai.description: This file implements the NegativeUNLVote class, which manages the voting process for the Negative Unique Node List (Negative UNL) in the XRPL consensus protocol. The Negative UNL is a mechanism to temporarily exclude unreliable validators from consensus without removing them permanently. The class provides methods to: 1) Collect and score validator performance over a configurable interval using validation history; 2) Identify candidates for disabling (adding to Negative UNL) or re-enabling (removing from Negative UNL) based on their reliability scores and protocol thresholds; 3) Randomly select candidates for action in a deterministic way; 4) Construct and add transactions to the ledger to modify the Negative UNL; 5) Track and manage new validators to avoid disabling them prematurely; 6) Log relevant actions and errors for debugging. The logic ensures that only validators with sufficient local validation activity participate in voting, and that the Negative UNL does not exceed protocol-defined limits. The class interacts with the ledger, validation records, and the transaction set to coordinate Negative UNL changes as part of the consensus process.

This file implements methods for the STValidation class in the Ripple (XRPL) protocol. It provides functionality for copying and moving validation objects, defines the format of a validation object (including required and optional fields), and implements methods to retrieve various fields such as signing hash, ledger hash, consensus hash, signing time, and seen time. It also includes methods to check if a validation is valid (by verifying the signature), if it is a full validation, and to retrieve the signature and serialized form of the validation. The code ensures that validations are properly formatted and cryptographically verified according to the protocol's requirements.

This file implements the configuration logic for the XRPL (Ripple) server. It provides platform-specific functions to determine system memory, parses INI-style configuration files, and manages configuration sections and values. The core class, Config, handles loading and interpreting configuration files, setting up directories, and initializing various server parameters such as node size, database paths, peer limits, network settings, and feature flags. The file includes validation and error handling for configuration values, supports environment variable overrides, and manages validator file loading and parsing. It also provides utility functions for retrieving configuration values, setting up fee voting parameters, and ensuring proper server setup based on the configuration. The design ensures robust, flexible, and platform-independent configuration management for the XRPL server.

This file implements the LedgerMaster class, which is a core component of the XRPL server responsible for managing the lifecycle, state, and history of ledgers. It handles tracking the current, validated, and published ledgers, manages ledger acquisition and validation, and coordinates the publication and storage of ledgers. The class ensures ledger continuity, handles missing or out-of-sync ledgers, and manages fetch packs for ledger synchronization between peers. It also processes held transactions, manages pathfinding requests, and interacts with other subsystems such as the order book database, fee tracking, and amendment management. The file includes logic for advancing the ledger state, handling consensus results, and maintaining caches and history for efficient ledger retrieval. It is central to the operation of the XRPL node, ensuring ledger integrity, synchronization, and network participation.

This file implements the PeerImp class, which represents a peer connection in the XRPL (Ripple) overlay network. PeerImp manages the lifecycle and communication of a peer, including connection setup, message sending and receiving, protocol negotiation, resource usage tracking, and feature support. It handles various protocol messages (transactions, validations, proposals, ledger data, etc.), manages transaction and ledger queues, enforces resource limits, and supports features like transaction reduce-relay, ledger replay, and squelching. The class also tracks peer metrics (latency, bytes sent/received), manages peer status and tracking (converged/diverged), and interacts with other network components such as the job queue, ledger master, validators, and resource manager. The file includes logic for relaying messages, handling protocol errors, charging peers for resource usage, and maintaining peer state for network health and synchronization.

This header file defines a set of invariant check classes used in the Ripple (XRPL) transaction processing engine. Each class represents a specific invariant that must be maintained during transaction application, such as ensuring no XRP is created, account roots are not improperly deleted, ledger entry types match, no bad offers or zero escrows are created, and various checks for NFTs, AMMs, and permissioned domains/DEXs. Each invariant checker provides visitEntry and finalize methods to inspect ledger changes and validate invariants after transaction execution. The file also defines a tuple type, InvariantChecks, aggregating all these checkers, and a function to instantiate them. These invariants help ensure ledger integrity and prevent protocol violations during transaction processing.

This file implements the core logic for the RCLConsensus class, which manages the consensus process in the Ripple (XRPL) ledger system. It defines the RCLConsensus and its nested Adaptor class, which acts as an interface between the consensus engine and the rest of the application. The Adaptor handles acquiring ledgers and transaction sets, sharing proposals and transactions with peers, proposing new ledgers, managing open transactions, and tracking consensus state. It also manages the process of closing and accepting ledgers, including building new ledgers, applying transactions, handling disputes, and validating ledgers. The file includes mechanisms for voting on fees and amendments, handling negative UNL (Unique Node List) votes, and detecting potential censorship of transactions. It provides detailed logging and status notifications to peers, and manages validator keys and operating modes. The RclConsensusLogger class is used for detailed timing and logging of consensus events. Overall, this file is central to the operation of distributed consensus in the XRPL node software, coordinating ledger agreement, transaction application, and network communication during consensus rounds.
